To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a DMRT model based on the Quasicrystalline Approximations with Coherent Potential was used to simulate brightness temperatures measured at the Local-Scales Observation Site of the Cold Land Processes Field Experiment, in Colorado.
the DMRT-QCA-CP model is a good tool for simulating brightness temperatures in a snowpack, when inputs are based on field-measured snow pit data.

the DMRT-QCA-CP model, with the best-fit snow grain size values as input parameters, is able to reproduce satisfactoily the brightness temperatures measured by GBMR-7 at the LSOS during IOP3 of the Cold-Land Processes Experiment.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a model that can be used to simulate the microwave emission of a snowpack, and with the validation of the model by comparing its output with measurements of the microwave emission of the snowpack.
the development of a new microwave radiative transfer model for snowpacks, which is able to predict the brightness temperatures at different frequencies.
the development of a new model for microwave emission from snowpack, based on the QCA-CP theory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the model was successful in reproducing the measured brightness temperatures, although the model's ability to simulate the measured data was limited by the lack of knowledge of the snowpack's stratigraphy and the presence of ice lenses.

the DMRT-QCA-CP model, with the snow particle radius as the only free parameter, is able to reproduce the measured GBMR-7 brightness temperatures, with a mean relative error of about 2.5%, and a maximum error of about 4%.

the DMRT model was able to simulate satisfactorily the brightness temperatures measured at the LS0S site by the Ground Based Microwave Radiometry system, with a best-fit snow particle size within the range of field-measured mean snow particle size.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the model can be used for simulating brightness temperature at LSOS, with the caveat that the snow pit measurements are not representative of the entire LSOS site.
the model was found to be able to reproduce satisfac- torily brightness temperatures measured at the LS0S.
the DMRT-QCA-CP model is a promising tool for the analysis of microwave data collected at high latitudes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DMRT-QCA-CP model can be used to simulate microwave brightness temperatures from snowpacks at different scales, and to retrieve mean particle radii, with a reasonable level of confidence.
the DMRT model, based on QCA-CP, is a useful tool to simulate microwave brightness temperatures at the LSOS, and that the snow pit measurements are a useful tool to constrain the model parameters.

a model like DMRT, based on QCA-CP, with a best-fit mean particle radius as input parameter, can be used to simulate the snowpack brightness temperatures at the three different frequencies of the GBMR-7 system, and that this model is a promising candidate to be implemented in a snow microwave radiative transfer model for operational snow mapping.
